HIAT: human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning with  auxiliary task
Bo Niu1 · Biao Luo1 · Yongzheng Cui1 · Xiaodong Xu1 · Yuqian Zhao1 · Yu Feng2
Artificial Intelligence Review (2025) 58:273 https://doi.org/10.1007/s10462-025-11260-4
Abstract Human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning (HIRL) tackles the challenges of inefficient  exploration and low sample efficiency by incorporating human feedback into the learn­ ing process to guide exploration and speed up learning. Nevertheless, most recent ap­ proaches overlook the problem of sample imbalance caused by varying behavioral policy  distributions in the early stages of training, which results in policy performance degrada­ tion due to biased learning toward dominant low-quality data. In this paper, we propose  a human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning method by constructing an auxiliary task,  namely Human-in-the-Loop Reinforcement Learning with Auxiliary Task (HIAT). Specifi­ cally, state-action pairs are utilized to create an auxiliary task that assesses the similarity  between different policies, forcing the model to focus on the differences in data sources.  The HIAT method guides the learning process of new policies during the policy evaluation  phase by implicitly influencing the assessment of different actions, thereby compensating  for sample imbalance. Subsequently, we introduce an adaptive weighting version, namely  adaptive weighting based HIAT (AWHIAT), which adjusts the impact of the auxiliary task  on the primary task based on their task-relevance and mitigates conflicts between different  tasks caused by cognitive load. Through empirical evaluations on six continuous control  benchmarks, the results demonstrate that AWHIAT significantly improves mean episode  reward and sample efficiency compared to four representative HIRL methods.
Keywords  Reinforcement learning · Human-in-the-loop · Deep learning · Auxiliary task
1  Introduction
Reinforcement learning (RL) uses exploration and trial-and-error mechanisms to learn  the optimal policy, solving sequential decision-making problems autonomously (Sutton  and Barto 1998; Hu et al. 2023). In recent years, deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has  emerged by combining RL’s credit assignment capabilities with the function approximation  potential of deep neural networks. This approach has achieved significant success in various  fields. For instance, it excels in industrial process control (Deng et al. 2023; Zheng et al.

However, RL is often criticized for its low sample efficiency  due to the trial-and-error mechanism and excessive ineffective exploration (Yu 2018; Zhu  and Zhao 2022).
Incorporating human prior knowledge has been proven to be an effective solution to  problems in existing RL algorithms (Perrusquúa et al. 2021). Human intervention skillfully  guides the agent towards deeper, more insightful exploration, thus significantly boosting  the efficiency of data sampling (Bobu et al. 2021). This approach is commonly known as  human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning (HIRL) (Warnell et al. 2018; Mandel et al. 2017).  The core idea of HIRL is to establish a feedback model that interacts with human experts  to facilitate the learning process of intelligent agents. Through the feedback mechanism,  human experts can express preferences for the current actions of the agent or directly pro­ vide demonstration actions for the agent to learn from. The training of the agent relies on  the interaction data between the agent and the environment, as well as the demonstration  data from human experts. Regrettably, the data obtained from the interaction of various  policies with environments are characterized by class imbalance, which adversely affects  the performance of HIRL. In HIRL interactions, actions are specifically generated by either  human or agent policies. Relative to agent actions, those originating from human policy are  superior in quality and thus carry significant instructional value. However, the quantity of  human actions is scarce due to the high costs associated with human labour. The volume  of data generated by the agent is higher; due to the trial-and-error nature of RL, the learn­ ing value of the data is diminished. The issue of class imbalance leads to the trained model  severely overfitting to the more abundant categories, neglecting the higher-quality data,  thereby resulting in a decline in the policy performance of HIRL. Therefore, balancing and  utilizing data effectively is crucial for enhancing the performance of HIRL.
Furthermore, human policy in HIRL is constrained by cognitive load, which signifi­ cantly affects the quality of demonstrations (Wu et al. 2023). As training duration increases,  humans face a growing cognitive load, resulting in reduced attention and suboptimal deci­ sion-making. This cognitive fatigue leads to a decline in human policy performance and  conflicts in HIRL’s optimization objectives. However, current HIRL approaches lack effec­ tive methods to address this issue.
One approach involves specifically having humans offer binary preferences for the data  derived from interactions. Subsequently, a reward function that incorporates these pref­ erence details is trained, avoiding direct intervention with the agent policy. This strategy  effectively mitigates the issue of class imbalance (Christiano et al. 2017; Cao et al. 2021).  However, this method struggles in more complex application scenarios where clear evalua­ tions are unattainable. It is difficult to quantify the information of different data trajectories  only in terms of good or bad in a complex environment, which can easily lead to misjudg­ ments by the agent. Additionally, there are supervised learning methods, including directly  modeling offline human demonstrations (Rajeswaran et al. 2018; Tangkaratt et al. 2020;  Hester et al. 2018). This approach requires a large volume of high-quality human demon­ strations for effective fitting. However, in most complex control domains, obtaining data  built by the optimal policy is challenging. Low-quality data is always inevitable, leading to  compound errors in models and resulting in poor generalization. Compared to the methods  mentioned above, constructing fitting auxiliary tasks for HIRL has more potential. In deep

learning, auxiliary tasks are utilized to tackle the challenge of class imbalance (Conneau and  Lample 2019; Lyle et al. 2021) and many studies have proven that transferring knowledge  from other auxiliary tasks can enhance the efficiency of RL (Lange et al. 2023; Xu et al.  2023). Due to conflicting optimization objectives, auxiliary tasks may not always be benefi­ cial to the primary task (Lin et al. 2019; Du et al. 2018). Additionally, there are no effective  auxiliary task construction methods for addressing the class imbalance issue in HIRL.
Inspired by the above discussion, we propose a new method for constructing human- in-the-loop reinforcement learning with auxiliary task (HIAT) to balance and utilize data  effectively, thereby enhancing the performance of HIRL. Specifically, we utilize the aux­ iliary task to learn the distinction between different policies, and then share the learned  representation with the primary task. Subsequently, to mitigate potential conflicts between  tasks and address the variable human policy quality caused by cognitive load, we introduce  an adaptive weighting version, namely adaptive weighting based HIAT (AWHIAT). This  approach dynamically adjusts the impact of the auxiliary task on the primary task based on  their task relevance, and can effectively compensate for conflicts in auxiliary task objectives  caused by cognitive fatigue. When human policy show inconsistencies typical of increased  cognitive load, AWHIAT recalibrates the weighting mechanism to maintain effective learn­ ing even under non-ideal human guidance conditions. Finally, we conduct comparative  evaluations with some HIRL algorithms in complex control environments. Our method  achieved significant improvements in terms of final performance, sample efficiency, and  stability in the MuJoCo experiments compared to existing state-of-the-art baseline methods.  For instance, HIAT demonstrated a 34.3% improvement in sample efficiency and a 7.02%  increase in average reward over 1000k timesteps compared to the best baseline algorithm  in the Ant environment, we also obtained competitive experimental results in several other  environments.
2  Related works
The current research on HIRL focuses on developing reward engineering to enhance learn­ ing efficiency. Specifically, interaction data is stored as trajectories, with humans offering  feedback categorizing them as good, bad, or neutral according to their preferences (Chris­ tiano et al. 2017; Cao et al. 2021). Agents utilize segments of these trajectories and feed­ back data to train reward engineering. Others have built upon this foundation to design  frameworks based on offline reinforcement learning (Kim et al. 2023). This method replaces  direct human intervention with additional human preference labels in the buffer. However,  the direct reward engineering framework by humans only obtains human preferences after  interactions and cannot acquire explicit human guidance in real-time to enhance exploration  efficiency. In contrast, our approach encourages agents to autonomously explore the envi­ ronment after acquiring certain capabilities, aiming to develop policy that surpass human  experts.
Unlike reward engineering, constructing auxiliary tasks for actors and critics is also con­ sidered a method to solve current problems (Lin et al. 2019; Lange et al. 2023). Some  related work involves constructing behavior cloning supervised learning auxiliary tasks in  the actor network using data from the human experience pool to achieve better performance  (Wu et al. 2023; Saunders et al. 2018). However, this has not yet been widely applied in the

HIRL domain. Unlike direct impacts on behavioral policy, critics’ auxiliary tasks improve  the Q-value estimation ability of the Q function, thereby indirectly influencing outcomes.  Some research also constructs auxiliary tasks for the critic network (Shelhamer et al. 2017;  Luo et al. 2024). Specifically, QDP is built from the perspective of the advantage function  as an auxiliary task for the critic network. QDP captures the relative effectiveness of human  expert Q-value actions and agent Q-value actions, timely correcting the network’s update  direction.
Our work is related to QDP in constructing auxiliary tasks for the critic network. How­ ever, our method not only obtains better network representation capabilities through shared  network layers, but also adjusts task weights according to the policy learning process. In  contrast, QDP relies entirely on the optimization gradient of auxiliary tasks throughout,  which may be affected by the optimization objective of the auxiliary task in the later stages  of training.
3  Preliminaries
3.1  Markov decision process
The RL problem is usually formulated as a Markov decision process (MDP) (Puterman  1990). It is defined by a tuple Μ = (Σ, Α, Ρ, Π, γ), where Σ represents the state space  describing all possible states in the agent’s environment, Α is the action space representing  all possible actions, Π indicates the state-transition probabilities, Ρ is the reward function  for state-action pairs, and γ is the discount factor. When the environment is complex or  not fully observable, trying to achieve Π is difficult; thus, agents interact with the environ­ ment by directly learning a policy π. This policy is typically learned through trial-and-error,  where the agent chooses an action a ∈Α according to its policy function a ∼π(s), leading  the environment to update its state to s′ ∈Σ and the agent receives a reward r ∼Ρ(s, a).  These empirical data are crucial to the agent’s learning process as they capture the essen­ tial information, allowing the agent to infer state transition probabilities accurately. Instead  of explicitly modeling the environment, the agent prioritizes continuous optimization of  expected returns. It interacts with the environment, gathering data as tuples (s, a, r, s′).  Considering the state-action pair (s, a) at a specific time step t, the return is characterized by  a discounted sum of future rewards

3.3  Reinforcement learning with auxiliary tasks
DRL algorithm must extract effective feature representations from a multitude of samples  when confronting complex tasks (He et al. 2023). Knowledge transfer across tasks signifi­ cantly enhances learning efficiency (Xu et al. 2023; Yin et al. 2024). Shared representations  of primary and auxiliary tasks are used in RL to introduce additional structure and informa­ tion, thereby optimizing the learning process. In the actor-critic framework, the primary task  is generally considered to be the actor’s decision-making or the estimation of the Q-value,  denoted as Τpri, alongside a set of auxiliary tasks labeled as a vector Taux. Λpri and Laux  are the optimization goals of primary task and auxiliary task, respectively. Within the RL  architecture, Λpri can either represent the expected return loss which is used for calculating  policy gradient, or the temporal difference error for Q-learning.
Our goal is to leverage the gradients from auxiliary tasks to more efficiently enable the  primary task to learn the features of the input, such as state s. By jointly training both tasks,  we aspire to achieve more efficient and effective learning outcomes. We utilize two distinct  neural networks for handling tasks: the first network, represented by parameters M(θ, φpri),  is dedicated to the primary task, while the second network, denoted as N(θ, φaux) focuses  on the auxiliary task. These networks share the parameters θ, while their task-specific  parameters are denoted as φpri and φaux. The following optimization objective is aimed to  be minimized:

where the vector ωT represents the weights of different auxiliary tasks. During the optimi­ zation process, the weighted loss of various tasks might positively influence early feature  learning but may diminish or become counterproductive with advancing training. If weights  are improperly allocated, excessive emphasis on certain auxiliary tasks will decelerate the

4  Method
In this section, we present our method HIAT, which adopts a joint training approach, using  auxiliary tasks to learn a representation containing human policy information for the pri­ mary task. In Sect. 4.2, to ensure that the primary task is not adversely affected by the  auxiliary task, we propose AWHIAT, which determines the weights of the auxiliary task by  considering the similarity between the gradients of the primary and auxiliary tasks.
4.1  HIAT: human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning with auxiliary task
As described in Sect. 3.2, to implement the HIRL algorithm, previous research has improved  the actor-critic framework by directly extracting historical tuples from the replay buffer Δ  during training. Based on the value of I(s), Δ can be categorized into the human buffer Δh  and agent buffer Δa. We aim to focus on the sparse data of Δh to enhance the performance  of HIRL.

4.2  AWHIAT: adaptive weighting for HIAT
In Sect. 4.1, the primary and auxiliary tasks are alternatively trained with equal weights of  1, implying that both tasks are of equal importance. In reality, our primary focus is on Τpri.  Moreover, HIAT does not take into account the impact of conflicts between tasks. Specifi­ cally, when the auxiliary discriminative task struggles to differentiate between human and  agent policy, it evidently affects the learning. In Sect. 3.2, we initially assume the human  policy to approximate optimal policy. The discrepancies between the current policy and an  optimal policy is identified through Τaux.
However, due to cognitive load constraints, human policy often deviate from theoreti­ cal optimality, especially in extended or complex tasks. As cognitive resources deplete,  human decision quality fluctuates due to fatigue, divided attention, and decreased motiva­ tion, making human demonstrations inconsistent. These cognitive limitations, combined  with the agent’s improving performance, result in human policies that increasingly diverge  from the true optimal policies as training progresses. Such discrepancies may impede the  learning of the primary task Τpri, that is, as agent policy improves, the performance differ­ ence between agent policy and human policy will gradually diminish, and may even surpass  the human policy. It becomes challenging to determine whether Τaux continues to advance  the learning of Τpri. Therefore, it is necessary to balance the optimization of the Τpri and  Τaux by adjusting weights, ensuring that the agent’s learning is not adversely affected by  the auxiliary tasks.
To address the above optimization problem, it is noted that both tasks have high relevance  when utilizing similar standards to evaluate state-action pairs. Besides, the learning of Τpri  is more challenging than Τaux. The auxiliary discriminative task is a coarse-grained task  with relatively lower learning difficulty, requiring binary classification of inputs. Unlike the  binary classification of Τaux, Τpri involves processing representations to generate estima­ tions of Q-values. Therefore, we propose a framework that dynamically adjusts the learning  weights λ and μ based on the learning difficulty. This adaptive approach also helps mitigate  the negative effects of cognitive load-induced inconsistencies in human demonstrations.  By dynamically adjusting the influence of human policy data based on its quality and con­ sistency, we can compensate for the varying reliability of human guidance throughout the  training process. In the initial stage of training, this approach prioritizes the coarse-grained  discriminative task to capture useful features effectively. Subsequently, the focus is shifted  towards policy evaluation in the later stages of the process. We define the task weighting λ  for Τpri as:

5  Experiments
In this section, we conducted extensive empirical and comparative experiments. Final  performance was assessed by measuring the average reward per episode, while sample  efficiency was evaluated based on the number of steps required to achieve optimal perfor­ mance. To ensure a fair assessment, all algorithms used the same set of hyperparameters,  as shown in Table 1, across all experiments. All experimental results are presented as the  mean and standard deviation of performance across different random seeds. All experiments  were performed on an Intel Xeon(R) Silver 4210R CPU and an NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPU.
Our framework was benchmarked in an online environment through a series of chal­ lenging and diverse continuous control tasks in MuJoCo (Todorov et al. 2012). The experi­ ments were carried out in six different MuJoCo environments: Inverted Double Pendulum,  Humanoid, HalfCheetah, Walker2d, Hopper, and Ant, aiming to assess sample efficiency  and performance.
When training the agent on the MuJoCo suite, the agent initially collects 20,000 states  and actions randomly to enhance exploration capabilities. The mean reward across three  episodes serves as a primary evaluation criterion. During the evaluation phase, exploration  techniques, such as injecting noise into actions in TD3, are not employed to maintain fair­ ness in algorithm assessment. This precaution is taken because such exploration strategies

Below is a detailed introduc­ tion to the algorithm:
IA-RL: A HIRL algorithm applied to Atari games, for which we implemented a QDP  version following the original paper. IA-RL trains a supervised learning head of a critic net­ work to predict whether the agent’s actions will lead the model into danger. This predictive  capability functions as an auxiliary learning task, enhancing the model’s safety awareness  and decision-making capabilities in complex environments.
Hug-RL: A HIRL algorithm applied to autonomous driving. The algorithm operates  through a dual-learning paradigm, enabling the agent to maximize expected return while  assimilating expert behavioral patterns.This synergistic approach facilitates accelerated  learning through expert imitation while maintaining the agent’s capacity for independent  decision-making and reward optimization.We implemented Hug-RL by incorporating the  active learning mechanism of QDP.
QDP: QDP represents a HIRL algorithm specifically engineered for continuous space  tasks. The algorithm’s fundamental premise lies in its dual-objective optimization: acceler­ ating the agent’s learning process through strategic human expert intervention while simul­ taneously minimizing the expert’s monitoring burden. This is achieved through a novel  Q-value-based advisory mechanism, where the agent autonomously solicits human exper­ tise during the initial training phase based on Q-value discrepancies, rather than depending  on continuous expert supervision. This approach effectively balances learning efficiency  with human resource optimization.
QDP+rwf (Lange et al. 2023): rwf constructs an auxiliary task for the Q-network to  predict the next step reward, aiding in the learning of Q-value estimation. Therefore, we  combine rwf with QDP as a standard, referred to as QDP+rwf.

5.2  Evaluations in representation
In this section, we explore whether AWHIAT can discern different quality (s, a) within the  representation Φ, as learned by the encoder. We have designed the following experiments to  verify that our algorithm, which trains with auxiliary tasks, learns a representation that can  distinctly differentiate data of varying quality in contrast to other algorithms.
For the experimental setup, we begin by randomly sampling data from the replay buffer.  The encoder, trained by each algorithm, is then applied to generate the representation Φ.  To visualize the structure of these encoded representations, we employ t-SNE (Maaten and  Hinton 2008), a widely-used dimensionality reduction technique. In the resulting visualiza­ tions, data points are colored according to their corresponding normalized reward values,  as depicted in Figs. 6 and 7. To provide a comprehensive comparison, we evaluate three  algorithms: TD3, QDP and AWHIAT trained for 300k and 1000k steps, respectively, under  identical conditions.
Analysis of Fig. 6 reveals that AWHIAT demonstrates a remarkable ability to differ­ entiate data quality after 1000k training steps. The t-SNE visualization exhibits distinct  clustering of data points, with each cluster occupying a unique region of the plot. These  clusters correspond closely to different reward levels, featuring well-defined boundaries and  minimal overlap. This clear separation underscores AWHIAT’s capacity to encode a repre­ sentation that effectively captures and distinguishes variations in data quality. In contrast,  the representations learned by TD3 and QDP exhibit less pronounced clustering, with data  points appearing more diffusely distributed and lacking the sharp delineation observed with  AWHIAT.
This trend becomes even more evident in the 300k-step experiment, as shown in Fig. 7.  At this earlier training stage, TD3 produces a representation with little to no discernible clus­ tering, suggesting an inability to meaningfully separate data by quality. QDP fares slightly  better but still lacks the clarity of AWHIAT. AWHIAT, however, displays a well-defined  transition band across reward values, with data points organized into coherent groups that  reflect their quality. This consistent separation, even with fewer training steps, highlights  the robustness of AWHIAT’s auxiliary task-driven training and its superior ability to learn a  structured and interpretable representation compared to the baseline methods.

6  Conclusions
In this article, we introduce auxiliary tasks into HIRL and propose a method called HIAT,  which mitigates the class-balance issue, effectively improving the algorithm’s performance  and sample efficiency. In the HIAT framework, the agent utilizes auxiliary tasks to distin­ guish between human and current agent policies. By sharing encoders, the agent integrates  representations learned from auxiliary tasks into policy evaluation, thereby facilitating the  learning process of the policy. Then, we introduce an adaptive weighting variant called  AWHIAT, which adjusts the impact of the auxiliary task on the primary task based on their  task-relevance. By adjusting weighting, the agent focuses on the auxiliary task during the  early stages of training, while ensuring the auxiliary task does not compromise the policy’s  convergence. In MuJoCo experiments assessing complex control tasks, our method sig­ nificantly enhances final performance and sample efficiency compared to existing state-of- the-art methods. In the Ant environment, HIAT showed a 34.3% improvement in sample  efficiency and a 7.02% increase in average reward over 1000k compared to the best base­ line algorithm. It also achieved competitive results in other environments. However, this  approach is currently limited to the actor-critic framework and requires real-time guidance.

DRL algorithm must extract effective feature representations from a multitude of samples  when confronting complex tasks (He et al. 2023). Knowledge transfer across tasks signifi­ cantly enhances learning efficiency (Xu et al. 2023; Yin et al. 2024). Shared representations  of primary and auxiliary tasks are used in RL to introduce additional structure and informa­ tion, thereby optimizing the learning process. In the actor-critic framework, the primary task  is generally considered to be the actor’s decision-making or the estimation of the Q-value,  denoted as Τpri, alongside a set of auxiliary tasks labeled as a vector Taux. Λpri and Laux  are the optimization goals of primary task and auxiliary task, respectively. Within the RL  architecture, Λpri can either represent the expected return loss which is used for calculating  policy gradient, or the temporal difference error for Q-learning.

Our goal is to leverage the gradients from auxiliary tasks to more efficiently enable the  primary task to learn the features of the input, such as state s. By jointly training both tasks,  we aspire to achieve more efficient and effective learning outcomes. We utilize two distinct  neural networks for handling tasks: the first network, represented by parameters M(θ, φpri),  is dedicated to the primary task, while the second network, denoted as N(θ, φaux) focuses  on the auxiliary task. These networks share the parameters θ, while their task-specific  parameters are denoted as φpri and φaux. The following optimization objective is aimed to  be minimized:

The encoder Eθ employs a alternating training strategy, wherein the learning of the auxiliary  task facilitates the encoder to acquire discriminative features that effectively distinguish  between human and agent policy distributions. This strategy ensures that each task main­

tains its operational independence within its designated network layer, thereby eliminating  potential cross-task interference. Gradient signals from the auxiliary discriminator G(•) are  leveraged to enhance the encoder’s ability to differentiate between state-action pairs origi­ nating from human demonstrations and those from the agent’s policy.

More significantly, the rich latent representation Φ learned through this optimization  process serves as a crucial knowledge bridge between the auxiliary and primary tasks. By  incorporating this shared representation, the Q-value estimation leads to more accurate  value assessments. In essence, HIAT creates a synergistic learning framework where the  shared encoder layers are incentivized to extract and utilize information that is beneficial for  both the discriminative auxiliary task and the primary RL objective.

In Sect. 4.1, the primary and auxiliary tasks are alternatively trained with equal weights of  1, implying that both tasks are of equal importance. In reality, our primary focus is on Τpri.  Moreover, HIAT does not take into account the impact of conflicts between tasks. Specifi­ cally, when the auxiliary discriminative task struggles to differentiate between human and  agent policy, it evidently affects the learning. In Sect. 3.2, we initially assume the human  policy to approximate optimal policy. The discrepancies between the current policy and an  optimal policy is identified through Τaux.

However, due to cognitive load constraints, human policy often deviate from theoreti­ cal optimality, especially in extended or complex tasks. As cognitive resources deplete,  human decision quality fluctuates due to fatigue, divided attention, and decreased motiva­ tion, making human demonstrations inconsistent. These cognitive limitations, combined  with the agent’s improving performance, result in human policies that increasingly diverge  from the true optimal policies as training progresses. Such discrepancies may impede the  learning of the primary task Τpri, that is, as agent policy improves, the performance differ­ ence between agent policy and human policy will gradually diminish, and may even surpass  the human policy. It becomes challenging to determine whether Τaux continues to advance  the learning of Τpri. Therefore, it is necessary to balance the optimization of the Τpri and  Τaux by adjusting weights, ensuring that the agent’s learning is not adversely affected by  the auxiliary tasks.

To address the above optimization problem, it is noted that both tasks have high relevance  when utilizing similar standards to evaluate state-action pairs. Besides, the learning of Τpri  is more challenging than Τaux. The auxiliary discriminative task is a coarse-grained task  with relatively lower learning difficulty, requiring binary classification of inputs. Unlike the  binary classification of Τaux, Τpri involves processing representations to generate estima­ tions of Q-values. Therefore, we propose a framework that dynamically adjusts the learning  weights λ and μ based on the learning difficulty. This adaptive approach also helps mitigate  the negative effects of cognitive load-induced inconsistencies in human demonstrations.  By dynamically adjusting the influence of human policy data based on its quality and con­ sistency, we can compensate for the varying reliability of human guidance throughout the  training process. In the initial stage of training, this approach prioritizes the coarse-grained  discriminative task to capture useful features effectively. A method based on the cosine similarity between the gradient updates of different tasks  is utilized to determine the appropriateness of the auxiliary task’s updates. This mechanism  is particularly valuable when human demonstrations become less reliable due to cognitive  fatigue. Specifically, when the cosine similarity is less than 0, it indicates a conflict between  two tasks. In such case, only the primary task’s loss should be updated. Conversely, when  no conflict exists, such as indicated by a non-negative cosine similarity, the primary and  auxiliary losses should be updated simultaneously.
